query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-temperature annealing combined with minor boron doping in high-entropy alloys forms a dense, self-healing oxide/passivation film that simultaneously retards mechanical wear and corrosion by stabilizing the protective surface layer under tribocorrosion conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited high-entropy alloy films with a less-dense, possibly amorphous or fine-grained microstructure lacking an optimized oxide/passivation film.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA films to high-temperature annealing (e.g., around 800 °C for a suitable duration) with low-level boron doping to promote the in situ formation of small boride particles and densification of the oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Testing under a coupled mechanical and corrosive environment (e.g., sliding under load in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) that induces both frictional wear and corrosive attack.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, continuous oxide/passivation film (augmented by in situ formed fine boride phases, such as TiB2-like particles) that acts as a physical barrier and exhibits self-healing characteristics during wear events.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature annealing promotes microstructural densification and recrystallization, while minor boron dopants react to form fine boride precipitates that refine the microstructure and enhance the integrity of the oxide film. This film effectively minimizes crack initiation and propagation and actively repassivates the surface after deformation, thereby resisting both mechanical abrasion and corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the treated HEA films will exhibit lower fluctuations in open circuit potential (OCP), reduced coefficient of friction, and lower wear rates compared to untreated films, with improvements attributable to the stable, self-healing oxide layer.
generation.baseline: HEA films processed without the combined heat treatment and boron doping, which typically develop less robust passivation layers and show higher wear and corrosive degradation under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction should hold under moderate to severe tribocorrosion conditions where the passive film can continuously reform. It may fail in excessively aggressive environments (for example, extreme pH or mechanical loads) or if the boron content is too high, causing oversized boride precipitates that introduce defects into the film.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of the boron-derived borides versus the thermal treatment in stabilizing the film, and the long-term durability of the self-healing behavior under cyclic loading, remain uncertain and require further systematic investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA film samples: one set with the combined high-temperature annealing and minor boron doping, and a control set without such treatment. Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion testing in a standardized environment (e.g., sliding under a defined load in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution for a fixed duration).
measurements: Real-time monitoring of open circuit potential (OCP) fluctuations
Coefficient of friction (COF) recording during sliding
Post-test surface characterization (SEM/EDS) of the oxide/passivation layer for density and continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated HEA samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements (i.e., reduced OCP fluctuations, lower COF, and lower wear rates) or if the post-test analysis reveals that the oxide/passivation film is not denser, more continuous, or lacks self-healing behavior relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. This study fabricated AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx HEA coatings on Q235 steel using laser cladding. By varying the amount of B added, the microstructure and mechanical properties of the coatings were enhanced. The key findings are as follows: (1) The coatings contain both BCC and σ phases. The addition of B did not alter the base phases in the coating, but it reacted with Ti in the molten pool to form TiB2 in situ. As B content increased, the BCC phase was refined, and both the proportion and size of TiB2 increased. (2) B addition improved the microhardness and wear resistance of the coatings. Microhardness increased with B content, and the coating with x = 1 exhibited the best wear resistance, attributed to the combination of a sufficient amount of small-sized TiB2 and solid solution strengthening. Excessive TiB2, especially large-sized particles, tends to spall during wear, exacerbating adhesive wear. (3) Compared to sample S1, the icorr value of sample S2 decreased by 51.0%, while Rf and Rct increased by 23.3% and 49.2%, respectively. reading.lever: Combine high-temperature annealing with minor boron doping to form a dense, self-healing oxide/passivation film.
reading.why: This approach, validated in related HEA films, directly targets simultaneous wear and corrosion by stabilizing the protective oxide layer under tribocorrosion conditions.
